Оба запускаются после рендера, но в разные моменты:

```txt
Рендер → Commit (React меняет DOM) → useLayoutEffect → браузер рисует → useEffect
```

`useEffect` запускается после того как браузер нарисовал кадр. Он асинхронен относительно рисования и не задерживает картинку. `useLayoutEffect` запускается сразу после того как React изменил DOM, но **до** того как браузер нарисовал кадр. Он задерживает рисование — и это нужно, когда надо замерить размеры и положение элементов (layout) и по этим замерам обновить состояние. Иначе пользователь на один кадр увидит элемент не на месте.

worst_places.after: No. They work differently. Debouncing delays the state update itself: the setter is not called until the timeout fires. `useDeferredValue` does not delay the update at all. It receives the already-updated value and tells React to render it at a lower priority. While that low-priority render runs in the background, the screen keeps showing the previous deferred value.

patterns: The Russian is a translation, not Russian writing, and it leaks in four recurring shapes: (1) English nouns declined with an apostrophe — «server component'ов», «Client'ом», «MouseTracker'ом», «Profiler'а», «fallback'ом», «date-picker'ов», «Provider'ы», «callback'а»; (2) bare English words used as Russian words mid-sentence — «нет mismatch», «memo'd», «до resolve», «in-flight Promise», «timing мог вызывать мерцание»; (3) invented transliterated verbs and nouns — «суспендит», «стримится», «Колокация»/«Коллоцировать», «стейтовая логика», «слайс», «битмаск-система»; (4) word-for-word calques that lose the meaning — «в полёте», «запрос в полёте», «CSS-содержание» (containment→contents, actively wrong), «Поресурсный» (route-based→nonsense), «Водопадов нет», «оставляя работу голодать», «изобретение колеса, плохо». Three of these — «в полёте», «опаковый»-style bare English nouns, and the invented verbs — are the identical defects already flagged in the react question bank, so this is a topic-wide translation habit and not a per-file slip.

The abbreviation habit from the question bank is reproduced exactly: DOM appears 90 times per locale across the 22 files and is expanded zero times; UI appears 17 times per locale and is expanded zero times. Add JSX, RSC, SSG, TTFB, SWR, SWC, CPU, ARIA, XSS, HOC — all used raw. Because articles are read out of order this bites hardest in file 11 (11 unexpanded acronyms in one file) and file 07 (DOM, SSG, TTFB plus «wire format», «shell», «payload», «server-only»).

Files 01-10 follow a good, consistent shape — lead sentence answers first, then a code block or ASCII diagram per idea, then a 'Типичные ловушки на интервью' block. File 11 breaks that shape completely: 3.6k RU / 4.4k EN words, 128 paragraphs, zero code blocks, zero diagrams, zero tables, every answer a single 60-100 word prose slab, and its own divergent Russian terminology («согласователь» for reconciler, «нарезка времени» for Time slicing, «лейаут» for layout, «слайс» for срез). It reads as if written by a different author from the ten articles that precede it, and it is the file a job-hunting reader will open last and trust most.

The Russian register switches hard mid-zone with no mixing inside any file: articles 01-07 address the reader as «вы» (8/8/2/5/2/6/3 hits, zero «ты»), articles 08-11 as «ты» (9/5/3/28 hits, zero «вы»). A reader moving from 07 to 08 is suddenly on informal terms with the text.

The English is consistently harder than the Russian, and the gap is widest exactly where sentences are longest: en/11 has 53 long sentences (19.6 % of all sentences, longest 67 words) against ru/11's 14 (5.2 %); en/10 has 10 (10.9 %) against ru/10's 3. The pattern is that a 'Common interview traps' answer is written as one paragraph of three or four sentences each carrying three or four facts, and the ~19 % word inflation of English pushes every borderline RU sentence over the limit.
notes: C (4.1) and E (4.4) are the zone's real strengths — leads answer first and code examples are self-contained, runnable and free of cross-example dependencies. Do not touch them. Three ASCII diagrams have broken box alignment and will wrap badly on a phone: the 'What runs where' two-column table in 07 (76 chars, and the EN version's `Run:` rows do not line up between columns), the flame-chart boxes in 08, and the linked-list traversal in 05 (Nav's sibling is drawn indented under Nav). Two content-level translation errors are worth a separate ticket, not just a language pass: «Поресурсный code splitting» (ru/08) and «CSS-содержание» (ru/09 twice, ru/11 once). One outright typo: «депроритизации» in ru/11 (should be «деприоритизации»); one gender-agreement error: «React Compiler (ранее называлась...)» in ru/10.
